862.title: The North American martyrs (1640s)
862.hook: Jesuits and lay helpers killed in the Great Lakes region, remembered with the harm of colonization
862.howItsDone: Catholics in the United States and Canada keep a feast of the North American martyrs, with shrines in New York and in Ontario, and some dioceses now pair it with prayer and education about Indigenous history.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kateri Tekakwitha, scarred by smallpox, walking to a mission near Montreal. Your line was lily of the mohawks. Did you learn the name of the people whose land you stand on? Today's story happened in those same forests, and it asks more of us. Day eight hundred sixty-two.

A French priest with mutilated hands kneels before an altar in France. His captors had cut and chewed his fingers, and the rules of the time said a priest's hands had to be whole to say Mass. Tradition says the pope gave him permission anyway. Then he did something hard to understand. He went back across the ocean, to the same country where he had been tortured, and he was killed there. His name was Isaac Jogues. He is one of a group the Church calls the North American martyrs.
screen: `A PRIEST WITH MUTILATED HANDS.` → `PERMISSION TO SAY MASS.` → `HE WENT BACK.`

segments.voice: First, who they were. Jesuit priests, among them Jean de Brébeuf and Isaac Jogues, and lay helpers like René Goupil and Jean de Lalande, who worked among the Wendat people, sometimes called the Huron, around the Great Lakes. They learned the languages, lived in the villages, and wrote long reports home. Brébeuf is remembered for a Christmas song in the Wendat language. Second, how they died. The Wendat and the Haudenosaunee nations, including the Mohawk, were at war, and the French were allied with the Wendat. The missionaries died in that war: some killed in raids, others tortured and killed after capture. Jogues wrote that Goupil was killed for making the sign of the cross over a child. Catholics honor them as martyrs, people who died for the faith they carried and would not abandon their missions. Jesus said it in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "Greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends." Third, the rest of the story. The missions came with European contact, and with it came diseases that emptied Native villages. Some Wendat blamed the missionaries. The missions were tied to a French colonial project that, over time, took land and power from Native nations. The Haudenosaunee were not villains in a saint's story; they were nations with their own reasons, their own alliances and their own dead. Fourth, holding both. Some Catholics in North America now speak of these martyrs alongside an honest account of colonization. Courage and harm sit in the same story. Remembering only one of them would be untrue to the other.
screen: `PRIESTS AND LAY HELPERS.` · `KILLED IN A WAR OF NATIONS.` · `DISEASE, LAND AND POWER.` · `COURAGE AND HARM TOGETHER.` · then, large: `LAY DOWN HIS LIFE FOR HIS FRIENDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold both stories. Settle, and breathe. In one hand, hold the missionaries: their courage, their love for the people they lived among, their deaths. In the other hand, hold the Native nations: the sickness that emptied their villages, the land taken, the wars made worse by powers from across the sea. Don't let one hand drop. Notice which one wants to. If you pray, you can pray for the dead on every side. If you don't, simply hold them all, without choosing. The bell holds the time.
Isaac Jogues. A Jesuit priest tortured and mutilated among the Wendat, who returned to the same country and was killed there, one of the North American martyrs.
Your line: remember all of it. Today, when you hear a proud story, from your country, your family or your faith, ask once who else was in the room. Day eight hundred sixty-two.

go back to the same country.

fork.reveal: he went back across the ocean, and he was killed there.

863.title: Francis de Sales (1567–1622)
863.hook: a gentle bishop who taught that everyone can be devout, in any job
863.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Francis de Sales, and his Introduction to the Devout Life is still read by laypeople; Salesian religious orders carry his name, and Catholic writers and journalists keep him as their patron.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the North American martyrs, among them Isaac Jogues, held together with the harm of colonization. Your line was remember all of it. When you heard a proud story, did you ask who else was in the room? Today we cross back to Europe, to a bishop in the Alps. Day eight hundred sixty-three.

Doors stay shut. A young priest has been sent into a region in the Alps where the people had become Protestant, and nobody wants to hear him preach. Some days he gets no audience at all. So he sits down and writes short leaflets, explaining the Catholic faith plainly, and tradition says he slipped them under doors. The Church now calls him a patron of writers and journalists. He would go on to become a bishop known less for winning arguments than for his gentleness. Today, Francis de Sales.
screen: `DOORS STAY SHUT.` → `LEAFLETS UNDER DOORS.` → `A PATRON OF WRITERS.`

segments.voice: First, a bishop without his city. Francis was named bishop of Geneva, but Geneva was a Calvinist city, so he lived and worked in nearby Annecy. He preached, heard confessions, and answered piles of letters from people trying to live their faith. Second, a book for everyone. Out of those letters came his Introduction to the Devout Life, addressed to a reader he calls Philothea, a name meaning one who loves God. His point: devotion is not only for monks and nuns. It must fit the life you actually have. A soldier, a shopkeeper, a servant, a married woman, a prince, each is devout differently. He compares it to bees, which take honey from flowers without spoiling them. Real devotion, he says, makes your work and your home better, not worse. Third, gentleness with yourself. In one chapter he warns against getting angry at yourself for your faults. When you fall, he says, don't rage. Pick yourself up gently, with sorrow but without fury, and begin again. Fourth, gentleness as strength. Tradition says Francis was hot-tempered by nature, and that his calm was hard won. That's why his gentleness meant something. It wasn't weakness; it was a temper held in a steady hand. Catholics hear his kind of gentleness in Jesus's words in Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "learn of me, because I am meek, and humble of heart."
screen: `BISHOP OF GENEVA, LIVING IN ANNECY.` · `DEVOTION FOR EVERY KIND OF LIFE.` · `DON'T RAGE AT YOUR OWN FAULTS.` · `A TEMPER IN A STEADY HAND.` · then, large: `MEEK, AND HUMBLE OF HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be gentle with yourself. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one fault from this week, something you said or didn't do. Notice how you usually talk to yourself about it. Is it a shout? A sigh? A long list? Now try it the way Francis advised: name the fault plainly, be sorry for it, and then speak to yourself the way you'd speak to a friend who made the same mistake. Then begin again. If you pray, you can hand the fault to God. If you don't, simply set it down. The bell holds the time.
Philothea. The name Francis de Sales gave the reader of his book, one who loves God, written to show that devotion can fit any kind of life.
Your line: gentleness is strength. Today, the next time you catch yourself in a mistake, lower your voice instead of raising it, inside and out. Day eight hundred sixty-three.

864.title: Jane Frances de Chantal (1572–1641)
864.hook: a widowed mother who founded the Visitation sisters with Francis de Sales
864.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Jane Frances de Chantal, and Visitation monasteries and schools carry on the community she founded with Francis de Sales; some parishes keep ministries for widows and the bereaved in her name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis de Sales, the bishop who wrote to Philothea that every kind of life can be devout. Your line was gentleness is strength. Did you lower your voice at a mistake of your own? Today, the woman who became his partner in that work. Day eight hundred sixty-four.

A hunting party in the French countryside. A shot goes wrong, and a nobleman is wounded by his own friend. Within days he is dead, and his young wife is a widow with small children and a grief that will not lift. For years she runs the household, cares for a difficult father-in-law, and prays without much comfort. Then, in Dijon, during Lent, she hears a bishop from Savoy preach, and something in her recognizes him. The widow is Jane Frances de Chantal.
screen: `A SHOT GOES WRONG.` → `A WIDOW WITH SMALL CHILDREN.` → `A BISHOP PREACHING IN DIJON.`

segments.voice: First, forgiveness. Tradition says Jane struggled for a long time to forgive the man who shot her husband, and that in the end she met him, and later stood as godmother to his child. It did not come quickly. That's part of why the story is told. Second, a friendship. Francis de Sales became her spiritual director, and their letters show a bishop and a widow, each helping the other toward God. They wrote about prayer, about her children, about his work, and about the quiet trust they shared. Some Catholics point to them as a picture of a holy friendship. Third, the Visitation. Together they founded a community of women called the Visitation, named for Mary's visit to her cousin Elizabeth in Luke's Gospel. It was meant for women whom the strict orders might turn away: widows, older women, women whose health could not take harsh fasting. At first, the sisters went out to visit the sick and poor. Church authorities then required them to live enclosed, and the community adapted, with prayer at its center. Fourth, widows. Jane knew from the inside what the letter of James says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Religion clean and undefiled before God and the Father, is this: to visit the fatherless and widows in their tribulation." She had been the widow in that line. She spent the rest of her life making a home for others.
screen: `FORGIVING THE MAN WHO FIRED.` · `A BISHOP AND A WIDOW, AS FRIENDS.` · `THE VISITATION: MARY TO ELIZABETH.` · `SHE HAD BEEN THE WIDOW.` · then, large: `VISIT THE FATHERLESS AND WIDOWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for widows, or keep one close in your thoughts. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who has lost a husband or wife. A grandparent, a neighbor, a friend's mother, someone from church, someone from the news. Let the empty side of their table be real for a moment. The meals for one. The decisions alone. If you pray, you can ask Jane Frances de Chantal to pray for them. If you don't, simply hold them, and notice whether a small way to visit them comes to mind. The bell holds the time.
Visitation. The community of women Jane Frances de Chantal founded with Francis de Sales, named for Mary's visit to her cousin Elizabeth in Luke's Gospel.
Your line: friends in god. Today, send one message to a friend who helps you be better, and tell them so. Day eight hundred sixty-four.

865.title: Vincent de Paul (1581–1660)
865.hook: a priest who organized charity across France
865.tomorrow: Louise de Marillac and the Daughters of Charity
865.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Vincent de Paul, and parish groups of the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul, named for him, visit people in need at home, run food pantries and thrift stores, and keep simple rules about how they serve.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jane Frances de Chantal, the widow who forgave, and the Visitation she founded with Francis de Sales. Your line was friends in god. Did you tell a friend they help you be better? Today, France again, and a priest with a different gift. Day eight hundred sixty-five.

Sunday morning in a small country parish. Just before Mass, someone tells the new priest about a family in a farmhouse outside town: everyone in it is sick, and nobody is looking after them. He mentions them in his sermon. That afternoon, it seems the whole parish walks out along the road with bread, soup and wine. It's beautiful. It's also chaos. Too much food arrives on one day, more than the family can use before it spoils, and next week they will be alone again. The priest watches and thinks: love needs a plan. His name is Vincent de Paul.
screen: `A SICK FAMILY OUTSIDE TOWN.` → `THE WHOLE PARISH SHOWS UP.` → `LOVE NEEDS A PLAN.`

segments.voice: First, the young Vincent. Tradition, and Vincent's own later words, suggest that as a young priest he wanted a comfortable post and a good income. He found work in a rich household as a tutor and chaplain, close to power. Second, the turn. Through that household he met the poor of the countryside: peasants dying without anyone to hear their confession, parishes without real priests. He began preaching missions in the villages, and gathered priests to do it with him. They became the Congregation of the Mission, and their motto came from Luke's Gospel, where Jesus reads from Isaiah. In the Douay-Rheims: "he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor." Third, the plan. After the day the whole parish showed up at the sick family's door, Vincent gathered the women of the town and wrote a simple rule: who goes on which day, what they bring, how they speak to the sick, how the money is kept. That small group, a Confraternity of Charity, became a model he spread to parish after parish. Fourth, the reach. He served as a chaplain to convicts chained to the oars of the king's galleys. He raised money from the wealthy for the hungry in war-torn regions. He worked with rich ladies and with poor country girls alike. Vincent's gift was not only compassion. It was the clipboard. He believed that charity done once, in a rush, can leave people worse off, and that charity with a schedule, a budget and a rule can last.
screen: `A YOUNG PRIEST WHO WANTED COMFORT.` · `PREACHING TO THE POOR.` · `THE RULE: WHO, WHEN, WHAT.` · `GALLEYS, WAR, HUNGER.` · then, large: `TO PREACH THE GOSPEL TO THE POOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: organize one good thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of a need near you that keeps coming back. A neighbor who needs rides. A friend who's grieving. A shelter that runs short at the end of the month. Now, instead of one big gesture, picture a small plan. Who could share it with you? Which day? What exactly would you bring? Let the plan get boring and specific. That's the point. If you pray, you can offer the plan to God. If you don't, simply let it take shape. The bell holds the time.
Confraternity. The group of women Vincent de Paul gathered in a parish with a simple rule for visiting the sick, a model he spread from town to town.
Your line: charity, organized. Today, put one good intention on a calendar, with a day, a time and a name next to it. Day eight hundred sixty-five.

screen: `DAY 865 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: LOUISE DE MARILLAC AND THE DAUGHTERS OF CHARITY.`

866.title: Louise de Marillac and the Daughters of Charity
866.hook: sisters without a cloister: the streets and hospitals were their convent
866.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Louise de Marillac, and the Daughters of Charity still work in hospitals, schools and among the poor; some Catholic social workers and nurses look to her as a patron.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vincent de Paul, who saw a whole parish bring too much food on one day and wrote a rule for a Confraternity. Your line was charity, organized. Did a good intention make it onto your calendar? Today, the woman who built that rule into a whole way of life. Day eight hundred sixty-six.

A young woman from the countryside arrives in Paris with a small bundle and one wish: to care for the poor and the sick. She has heard that a lady here trains girls for that work. The lady who takes her in is a widow of noble birth, anxious by temperament, who once wanted to be a nun and was turned away. Together they are about to build a community of women who serve God with no convent walls. Today, Louise de Marillac and the Daughters of Charity.
screen: `A COUNTRY GIRL AT THE DOOR.` → `A WIDOW WHO WAS TURNED AWAY.` → `NO CONVENT WALLS.`

segments.voice: First, Louise. She was born to a noble family but outside marriage, and grew up never quite belonging. She asked to enter a strict convent and was refused, partly for her health. She married, had a son, nursed her husband through a long illness, and was left a widow, troubled by doubt and worry. Second, Vincent. Vincent de Paul became her spiritual director, and he gave her work: visiting the charity groups he had started in the parishes, checking their accounts, encouraging the volunteers. She was good at it. She saw what the noble ladies could not do themselves: the daily, dirty, tiring care of the sick at home. Third, the Daughters. Country girls began coming to serve, and Louise took them into her own house to train them. That was the beginning of the Daughters of Charity. To keep them free for the streets, they were not set up as an enclosed order. Vincent put it to them in words they remembered, paraphrased here: your convent is the houses of the sick, your cell a rented room, your chapel the parish church, your cloister the streets of the city. Fourth, the work. They nursed in hospitals, cared for abandoned babies, visited prisoners, taught poor girls. When a lawyer in Luke's Gospel asks who his neighbor is, Jesus tells the story of the Samaritan on the road and ends, in the Douay-Rheims: "Go, and do thou in like manner." The Daughters took that road as their cloister.
screen: `NEVER QUITE BELONGING.` · `VINCENT GIVES HER WORK.` · `COUNTRY GIRLS IN HER HOUSE.` · `HOSPITALS, BABIES, PRISONS.` · then, large: `GO, AND DO THOU IN LIKE MANNER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: serve someone on the street, or get ready to. Settle, and breathe. Think of the streets you'll walk or drive today. Who is out there? Someone asking for change at a corner. A person sleeping in a doorway. A delivery worker in the rain. Pick one. Ask what a small act of service might look like: a greeting, a bottle of water, a meal, a real look in the eye. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name or by face. If you don't, simply hold them, and plan the small act. The bell holds the time.
Louise. The widow Vincent de Paul trained to run his charity groups, who later gathered country girls into her own house to found the Daughters of Charity.
Your line: the street is the cloister. Today, treat one ordinary sidewalk, hallway or bus as holy ground, and serve one person you meet there. Day eight hundred sixty-six.

867.title: The Sacred Heart (1673–1675)
867.hook: Margaret Mary Alacoque sees the heart of Christ burning with love
867.howItsDone: Catholics keep images of the Sacred Heart in homes and churches, some consecrate their families to it, parishes keep first Friday devotions, and the Church keeps the Solemnity of the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus each year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Louise de Marillac and the Daughters of Charity, sisters whose convent was the city. Your line was the street is the cloister. Who did you serve out there? Today we step back inside a convent wall, into one quiet chapel. Day eight hundred sixty-seven.

A chapel in Paray-le-Monial, a small town in France. A nun of the Visitation, the order founded by Francis de Sales and Jane Frances de Chantal, whom we met a few days back on this path, is kneeling in prayer before the Blessed Sacrament. Her name is Margaret Mary Alacoque. She later wrote that Jesus showed her his heart: burning with flames, ringed with thorns, a small cross rising from it. She wrote that he spoke of a heart that loved people so much and received so little love in return. She told her superiors. They doubted her. Today, the heart she said she saw.
screen: `A CHAPEL IN PARAY-LE-MONIAL.` → `A HEART IN FLAMES.` → `HER SUPERIORS DOUBT HER.`

segments.voice: First, the picture. You may have seen it on a holy card, in a kitchen, above a church door. A heart, on fire. Thorns around it. A cross on top. Often a wound in it, and Jesus pointing to it with his own hand. In the Bible the heart isn't only feelings. It's the whole inner person, where a life is decided. So for Catholics the Sacred Heart is Christ's love itself, human and divine, made visible. Second, it's older than the chapel. Catholics root it in the Gospel of John, at the cross. In the Douay-Rheims: "one of the soldiers with a spear opened his side, and immediately there came out blood and water." An opened side. A heart left open. Third, the nun who wasn't believed. Margaret Mary's own superiors weren't sure what to make of her. Then a Jesuit, Claude de la Colombière, was sent to the convent as confessor. He listened, came to trust her, and encouraged her to write down what she had received. What she wrote asked for simple things: receiving communion on the first Friday of the month, keeping watch in prayer for an hour, and a feast day for the heart of Christ. Later, the Church made that feast its own. Fourth, the fire. In Luke's Gospel, Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am come to cast fire on the earth; and what will I, but that it be kindled?" The flames in the picture answer that line. Some people find the statues too sweet. Catholics who keep the devotion say it isn't sweet at all: it's about a love that keeps burning when it's refused.
screen: `A HEART ON FIRE, THORNS, A CROSS.` · `AN OPENED SIDE AT THE CROSS.` · `A JESUIT CONFESSOR BELIEVES HER.` · `FIRE CAST ON THE EARTH.` · then, large: `I AM COME TO CAST FIRE ON THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at an image of the Sacred Heart. If there's one in your home or a church nearby, go and stand in front of it. If not, find a painting on your phone. Settle, and breathe. Let your eyes move slowly: the flames, the thorns, the cross, the wound, the hand that points to it. Then let them rest on one detail and stay there. Don't analyze. Just look. If you pray, you can say his words from Luke under your breath: that it be kindled. If you don't, simply notice what that one detail says to you. The bell holds the time.
Cor Iesu. Latin for heart of Jesus, the words that open most invocations in the Litany of the Sacred Heart, Christ's love pictured as a heart on fire.
Your line: a heart on fire. Today, every time you see a heart, on a text, a sign or a coffee cup, let it point you back to the burning one. Day eight hundred sixty-seven.

what it means: Christ's love, human and divine, pictured as a heart that keeps burning even when its love is refused.

868.title: Jansenism
868.hook: a strict movement kept people from communion; the Church later encouraged frequent communion
868.howItsDone: Catholics who are free of grave sin are encouraged to receive communion often, even daily, and before receiving they say together a form of the centurion's words from Matthew 8:8, confessing they are not worthy and asking only for a word of healing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sacred Heart, Cor Iesu: a nun in Paray-le-Monial, a Jesuit who believed her, and a love that keeps burning when it's refused. Your line was a heart on fire. Did a heart catch your eye somewhere? Day eight hundred sixty-eight.

"Lord, I am not worthy." At Mass, just before communion, Catholics say a line borrowed from a centurion, an army officer, in the Gospel of Matthew. In the Douay-Rheims he says: "Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof: but only say the word, and my servant shall be healed." Two halves. I'm not worthy. Only say the word. Now suppose someone took the first half so seriously they never reached the second. Suppose they decided the table was for people who had finally earned it, and stayed in the pew, week after week, waiting to be good enough. Today, a movement that pulled people in that direction.
screen: `LORD, I AM NOT WORTHY.` → `BUT ONLY SAY THE WORD.` → `STUCK ON THE FIRST HALF.`

segments.voice: First, a book. Cornelius Jansen was a bishop in Flanders who spent years studying Saint Augustine on grace. His long book on Augustine came out after his death, and the movement that followed took his name: Jansenism. It painted fallen human nature in very dark colors, and it was severe about who could be saved. Popes later condemned propositions drawn from the book. Second, a convent. The Cistercian nuns of Port-Royal, near Paris, became the movement's heart. A theologian close to them, Antoine Arnauld, wrote a book on frequent communion that urged long preparation and real penance before receiving. The philosopher Blaise Pascal took their side in a public quarrel. These were serious, prayerful people, and they wanted reverence. Third, the cost. In practice, communion started to look like a reward for the nearly perfect. Some Catholics went a long time without receiving, afraid they never would be worthy. Fear of sin began to crowd out trust in mercy. Fourth, the Church's answer. Over time, Rome pushed the other way. Pope Pius X urged Catholics to receive often, even daily, and opened communion to young children. Pope Francis has written that the Eucharist is not a prize for the perfect but medicine and food for the weak. The Church still asks anyone aware of grave sin to go to confession first. That isn't Jansenism. It's a door, not a wall. Jesus said it plainly in Matthew: "They that are in health need not a physician, but they that are ill."
screen: `A BISHOP'S BOOK ON GRACE.` · `PORT-ROYAL: PREPARE, THEN WAIT.` · `COMMUNION AS A REWARD.` · `MEDICINE FOR THE WEAK.` · then, large: `THEY THAT ARE IN HEALTH NEED NOT A PHYSICIAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: receive without keeping score. Settle, and breathe. If you receive communion, think of the next time you will. Notice any voice that says you haven't earned it yet, and answer it with the whole of the soldier's line, both halves. If you don't receive communion, bring to mind one gift you were given that you felt you didn't deserve: a kindness, a second chance, a meal. Hold it like a gift, not a debt. Let it stay unearned. The bell holds the time.
Jansenism. A strict movement named for Bishop Cornelius Jansen, severe about grace and wary of frequent communion, which the Church came to resist.

Your line: not a reward. This week ran from martyrs remembered honestly, through a gentle bishop and his friend, charity organized and sisters on the street, to a heart on fire and today's open table. Today, take one good thing without trying to earn it. Day eight hundred sixty-eight.

fork.setup: you're a Catholic who has been to confession, but you still feel you're not good enough. Sunday comes. what do you do?
options: stay in the pew until you feel perfect.
receive, trusting it's food for the weak.
stop going to Mass at all.
fork.reveal: the Church's answer, against the Jansenist mood, is to receive. the Mass even has you say 'I am not worthy' right before you do.

original.note: Latin: Lord, I am not worthy, the centurion's words from Matthew 8:8, said before communion.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old argument about a bishop nobody remembers.
what it means: a strict movement that made communion feel like a reward for the nearly perfect, and kept people away.
what a scholar hears: Jansen's book on Augustine, the nuns of Port-Royal, Arnauld on frequent communion, Pascal in their defense, and Rome's long turn the other way.

sources.ref: Sacra Tridentina Synodus (decree on frequent and daily communion) and Quam singulari (on first communion of children), under Pius X
